meta.title: Tagalog A1 Beginner
meta.subtitle: 500 words · both directions, as two cards per word
meta.desc: Both study directions in one deck: Tagalog → English (see the Tagalog, recall the meaning) and English → Tagalog (see an English meaning, recall the Tagalog). Each direction is a card of its own with its own schedule, so recognising a word and producing it are learnt separately. 500 words for a beginner, aligned to A1 of the Common European Framework of Reference, whose global descriptor begins 'Can understand and use familiar everyday expressions and very basic phrases aimed at the satisfaction of needs of a concrete type' — a learner here is able to introduce themselves and others, to ask and answer questions about personal details such as where they live, people they know and things they have, and to interact in a simple way provided the other person talks slowly and clearly and is prepared to help. WHERE THESE WORDS COME FROM, since it matters: this deck is not any examination's vocabulary and does not claim to be — Tagalog has no CEFR examination, and no openly licensed graded word list was found to build it from. It is assembled from two things that can be stated. 360 of the 500 come from a vocabulary written for the level's scope — greetings and politeness, introducing yourself, family, numbers, telling the time, days and months, food and drink, shopping and money, the home, the town and getting about, the body and feeling ill, the weather, colours, and the pronouns, markers, question words, particles and conjunctions every sentence is built out of — and the other 140 are the commonest remaining words, by a frequency that averages two sources: a word list built from film and television subtitles, and the Tagalog sentences of Tatoeba, each counted per million words. The cards are dealt by that frequency, so the words you meet most often come first. Every headword is spelt as ordinary Tagalog writing spells it, and beneath it Wiktionary's pronunciation in the International Phonetic Alphabet (496 of the 500) and, where the word carries one, its marked spelling, because ordinary writing shows neither the stress nor the final glottal stop (bata, a child, is batà). Verbs are given as the affixed verb you say (kumain, to eat), and the 95 verbs show their three aspects — completed, ongoing and contemplated (kumain, kumakain, kakain) — since Tagalog marks whether an action is done rather than when; where Wiktionary names it, a word shows its root and affix (kain + -um-). Real example sentences come with 492 of the 500 words, three apiece for 479 of them, with the word picked out in colour and a speaker beside the sentence and the headword. Sources. Level: the Common European Framework of Reference (Council of Europe), global scale. Meanings, spellings, aspects and pronunciation: English Wiktionary, via the kaikki.org extraction (CC BY-SA 4.0). Frequency: a word list built from OpenSubtitles (hermitdave/FrequencyWords, CC BY-SA 4.0) and the Tatoeba corpus. Example sentences: Tatoeba (tatoeba.org), CC BY 2.0 FR.
